issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette:
Daniel, a 32-year-old European American tutor, came for help after nearly a year of living as though the world had become a place of hidden approaches and unreadable intentions. The stalking began with a man who first seemed merely persistent: waiting near Daniel’s train stop, appearing again outside the café where he marked essays, leaving messages that were vague enough to be denied and specific enough to be frightening. Because Daniel already felt danger as something that could emerge from almost anywhere, those moments quickly took on the quality of signals rather than coincidences. A parked car in the wrong place, a familiar route that suddenly felt exposed, or the sense that someone had been looking his way became the kind of cues he could not dismiss. It escalated over weeks into a pattern Daniel could not predict, and the uncertainty mattered as much as the contact itself. He began to believe that other people were not what they seemed, that people could not be trusted, and that he could not trust himself to do the right thing if something similar happened again. What troubled him most was how quickly ordinary encounters started to feel contaminated by that experience. Once Daniel had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he could not trust his own judgment, almost anything could tip into a warning: a figure lingering at the edge of his vision, a tone of voice that seemed just slightly wrong, or footsteps behind him on the pavement. Living at that pitch of threat, he found the city dense with reminders he could not stop reading. If a colleague’s tone sharpened in a staff room, or if a parent sounded even calmly annoyed about a cancelled tutoring session, Daniel felt a jolt of alarm and read danger into the situation. The same happened with the sudden whine of a motorcycle passing his flat, or the sense of being watched when he crossed unfamiliar streets after work; his mind went immediately to the possibility that someone was tracking him, and those moments fed his conviction that the world was full of concealed threats.

As those interpretations hardened, Daniel’s ways of coping narrowed. He pulled back from emotional closeness with his wife, saying that intimacy now felt unsafe because once he let himself relax, he might stop noticing warning signs. He avoided unwinding in the evenings, keeping himself busy with work emails, news, or household tasks because quiet felt like an invitation for something bad to happen. He also turned on himself, telling himself he deserved to suffer because of what had happened, as if vigilance and discomfort were a fitting penalty for not having prevented the stalking or for not responding “correctly” enough. That self-punishing stance did not soothe him; it deepened his belief that he was not someone who could be relied on. In turn, it made him even more guarded, more certain that closeness, ease, and trust were luxuries he could not afford.

Over time, the cost of living that way began to shape his days. Daniel stopped taking new tutoring jobs in neighborhoods he did not know, because unfamiliar places left him unable to assess danger and he found himself scanning exits, cars, and faces instead of focusing on his students. He planned routes obsessively, arrived early to avoid feeling cornered, and sometimes declined appointments that seemed too out of the way. At home, the house never quite became restful. He fell asleep late after checking locks and windows, and he woke easily, certain for a few seconds that something was wrong even when nothing was. The false alarms left him exhausted, and the exhaustion made it harder to think clearly the next day, which only strengthened his sense that he could not trust himself to make the right judgment under pressure. His marriage began to feel the strain of his distance; his wife noticed that he was present in the room but rarely fully with her, and Daniel admitted that emotional closeness now felt like standing unprotected in open ground.

The more he arranged his life around caution, the more he encountered the very cues that kept the fear alive. A motorcycle revving at the corner outside his building could derail his concentration for the rest of the afternoon. An irritated parent on the phone could make his pulse race and send him back into the old certainty that anger from another person meant trouble was coming. A new street, a new student’s neighborhood, or the experience of noticing someone walking a little too steadily behind him on the sidewalk would make him scan harder, feel more exposed, and then feel ashamed of himself for being unable to settle. By the time he sought therapy, Daniel was not only frightened of being harmed again; he was frightened that his own vigilance had become the only thing keeping him functioning, even as it kept him trapped. He came because he was tired of living in constant alertness and because he did not want his marriage and work to shrink further, but he was most afraid that if he stopped protecting himself in this way, he would miss the next warning and never recover from it.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs and appraisals, but it does not clearly say they trigger or give rise to specific reminders/cues in the same paragraph.
The vignette includes a sense of danger, but it does not explicitly portray that perceived threat generates the triggering stimuli/reminders themselves.

- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows negative beliefs and appraisals, but it does not clearly say they trigger or give rise to specific reminders/cues in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."

  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
